### HT Cultivation Systems

Cell cultivations and product formation under a vast number of parameters and process conditions strongly influence the product purification process [47]. The screening for optimal expression systems, media, additives, process conditions, and induction setups for up- and downstream applications explains the need for cultivation systems in miniaturized format. The first overview of different commercial micro-cultivation systems and their specifications are shown in

Table 1. While such HT systems are operated with small-volume reactors, many of these systems lack in process control compared to fully equipped bioreactors [48]. Cultivations in standard 96-well microtiter plates (MTPs) represent the optimal system for miniaturization while reducing the process information content to a minimum [49]. Ninety-six well approaches in standard MTPs were used for the rapamycin production in Streptomyces hygroscopius [50], Glucansucrase from Leuconostoc mesenteroides mutants [51], and recombinant human protein 1 from Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells [52]. Small-scale stirred vessels [53-56] and bubble columns [57,58] bypass such losses in process information, whereas such systems rather represent a medium-throughput approach. The Advanced Microscale Bioreactor (ambr) by Sartorius Stedim Biotech is an ideal HT tool for upstream processing (USP) development as it combines high process information and control as well as low material consumption and culture volume. The ambr system consists of 24 or 48 parallel bioreactors of 10-15 mL, integrated into a fully automated robotic workstation, which enables feeding strategies and sampling. Each cultivation block can be individually tempered, aerated, and mixed while monitoring the oxygen uptake and the culture pH via optical sensors [59]. The mixing and aeration is realized by a small-scale hollow impeller within each bioreactor. The ambr system was used in diverse studies such as in upstream optimizations for mAbs from CHO cells [60, 61] as well as for experiments involving hematopoietic stem cell cultures [59]. A system comparable to the ambr technology allowing for cultivations in the 8-15 mL scale in 48-well format was introduced by Riedlberger and Weuster-Botz [62, 63] and commercialized by 2mag as the bioreactor 48 system. Using this system, highcell density yeast cultivations for an optimized production of Candida antarctica lipase B was realized [64]. An alternative system, which is frequently used for experiments involving microbial cells, is the BioLector system (m2p-Labs). The upstream optimization is performed in continuously shaken 48-well plates, which were geometrically optimized for culture mixing and oxygen supply into the medium [65]. The BioLector cultivation plates are all equipped with an optical bottom, enabling quasi-continuous cell density and product measurements without additional sampling procedures [66]. Analogously to the ambr system, such cultivation plates are available with optical sensors for the determination of culture pH and oxygen transfer rates [67]. In the RoboLector setup (a combination of the BioLector and a fully automated liquid handling station) as used by Huber et al. [68], different feeding and induction strategies can be realized. Similar experiments were performed by Funke et al. [69], using a microfluidic BioLector derivative. This HT cultivation device can be found widely in the literature, e.g. in product formation studies for Corynebacterium glutamicum [70,71] and Hansenula polymorpha [72]. Scalability of the results in miniature scale can be ensured by the sulfite oxidation method guaranteeing a constant oxygen transfer rate between two scales [73].

### HT Cell Lysis Systems

For bacterial hosts such as Escherichia coli, the commonly intracellular products need to be released from the cytoplasm. As HT cultivation strategies can result in a bottleneck at the product extraction stage, HT-compatible cell lysis systems need to be considered. Mechanical cell breakage systems such as bead mills were scaled down to the milliliter scale using beating beads (e.g. NucleoSpin bead system by Macherey-Nagel) agitated by simple mixing. Such a procedure was used for the characterization of bacteria from the human oral and gastrointestinal tract [74,75]. Also, physical cell lysis systems such as sonication devices were adapted to HT compatibility by using multi-tipped horns for cell breakage in MTP format. A 24-well HT sonication device was used by Hohnadel et al. [76] for 15 distinct cell types including gram-negative and -positive bacteria as well as fungi and yeasts. An eight-well sonifyer for the release of virus-like particles from E. coli was used by Ladd et al. [77]. Another physical HT cell breakage system based on electric fields in parallel microfluidic channels was developed by Poudineh et al. [78]. The system introduces strong electric fields into the fluid by multiple sharp-tipped three-dimensional electrodes and was successfully applied for extracting intracellular molecules from E. coli. Physical cell lysis in the full 96-well format can also be realized by straightforward temperature treatment, osmotic shocks, and freeze drying [79]. The full capacities of HTPD in microtiter format can be achieved in terms of chemical (e.g. detergents, solvents, alkaline pH, etc.) and biological (phages, enzymes, etc.) cell lysis. The harvested cells can be re-suspended in the respective chemicals analogously to the large scale [79]. The chemical and biological treatment strategies can be easily implemented into fully automated robotic work stations as shown by Listwan et al. for proteins expressed in E. coli [80]. As different strategies for soluble and insoluble protein expression exist, even conditions of IB formation can be identified, e.g. by using trichloro acetic acid-acetone total protein extraction protocols [81].

### HT IB Refolding

IBs, being denatured highly pure product aggregates formed in E. coli cells, are a special case in biopharmaceutical process development. Designing IB refolding strategies can be highly feasible especially for rather small proteins such as insulin. The entire process of IB unfolding, protein refolding, and isolation of the correctly folded species is not straightforward, making HTPD the method of choice for designing such processes. An IB refolding process for a fully automated robotic workstation for lysozyme and different proteins from E. coli were introduced by Berg et al. [82], Vincentelli et al. [83], and Dechavanne et al. [84]. The protein unfolding and refolding process included investigation of different pH ranges, salts, as well as additives like DTT, glutathione, folding enhancers (chaperones), glycerol, PEG, and co-factors. In many fundamental studies on protein unfolding and refolding, certain types of additives and chemical buffers were classified as ideal. As a consequence, different commercially available HTPD refolding kits are available such as the QuickFold system (Athena Enzyme Systems) [85], the Pro-Matrix system (Thermo Scientific) [86], the iFOLD kit (Merck Biosciences) [87], and the FoldIt Screen kit (Hampton Research) [88].

### HT Purification Systems

Both for intracellular and extracellular products as well as for refolded protein species in a mixture of correctly and falsely folded proteins, a purification strategy is mandatory for meeting the requirements stated by the authorities. The first overview of different HT downstream screening systems and their specifications is shown in

Table 2. As many unit operations in the biopharmaceutical industry require defined buffer conditions, different miniaturized devices are available. For buffer exchange and diafiltration, PD desalting columns (GE Healthcare Life Sciences) [89,90], Slide-A-Lyzer Dialysis cassettes (Thermo Scientific) [77,91], and the Pierce 96-well Microdialysis Plate (Thermo Scientific) [92] are widely applied in academic research. Vivaspin centrifugal concentrators (Sartorius AG) even enable ultrafiltration and sample concentrations in sub-milliliter format with different molecular-weight cutoff membranes [93,94].

#### HT Solubility Screenings

Selective protein precipitation is a very straightforward and scalable downstream unit operation for enhancing product purity. As a prerequisite for selectively removing certain species, the solubility lines of products or impurities need to be determined. Different HT screening methods for investigating colloidal stability and protein phase behavior can be found in the literature. Wiendahl et al. [95] developed an MTP-based method for protein precipitation based on fast liquid evaporation in micro-scale format. In case studies for lysozyme and insulin variants, systems of different protein and precipitant concentrations were pipetted on a fully automated liquid handling station. After different time frames of liquid evaporation, the turbidity as well as the filling volume were determined until crossing of the solubility line. The presented technology enables the determination of different points within the phase diagram starting from one single starting condition. Different 96-well filter plates such as the MultiScreen Assay System (Merck Millipore) [96] and the Chromafil Multi

96 Filter Plates (Macherey-Nagel) [97] were used for solubility investigations for pharmaceutical drug candidates and membrane proteins. An apparatus originally used for screening of crystallization conditions is also used for investigating long-term protein phase behavior including effects within the metastable and labile regions of the phase diagram. This technology was used for identifying different aggregate states such as precipitate, crystals, skin formation, gelation, and liquid-liquid phase separation for an mAb [98] and different model proteins [99]. This methodology can thus not only be used for simple precipitation and solubility screens but can also be seen as a linking technology between

#### HT Aqueous Two-Phase Systems

Another unit operation used in early stages of product purification is aqueous two-phase partitioning. Two bio-compatible and non-miscible aqueous phases composed of salts (phosphate, sulfate), sugars (dextran), or biopolymers (PEG) are mixed with a complex cell lysate. The different biomolecules are then either dragged to the top, bottom, or inter-phase, which results in a purification effect depending on the distribution behavior. HT technologies can be used for characterization of the aqueous two-phase systems for the determination of bimodal curves (region of phase separation) and conodes (lines of equal top and bottom phase composition) for different salts and polymers as introduced by Bensch et al. [101]. When the systems are characterized, different partitioning studies for biomolecules can follow as shown for model proteins like lysozyme and pharmaceutically relevant molecules such as mAbs [102] and virus-like particles from human B19 parvo-virus [103].

#### HT Chromatography

Chromatography is one of the most commonly used unit operations within biopharmaceutical DSP during all stages of process development. Therefore, a large number of screening platforms were developed covering batch resin screenings and dynamic binding systems like miniaturized chromatography columns. Screening for binding and elution conditions as well as comparing different adsorbent media is mostly performed in 96-well filter plates. Batch binding and elution experiments for kinetic and isotherm studies were applied for mAbs and Fc fusion proteins [104], α-amylase and scFv-β-Lactamase fusion protein [105], and the angiotensin-II generating enzyme [106] in different IEX and HIC setups in standard filter plates. Pre-packed PreDictor filter plates (GE Healthcare Life Sciences) are limited to certain adsorbent types and a standard adsorbent volume and were used for bind-elute screenings for mAbs and amyloglucosidase [107,108]. By contrast, the MediaScout ResiQuot system (Atoll) allows for a flexible generation of equally sized adsorbent plaques for self-packed adsorbent plates [109]. The plaques are generated by applying vacuum to adsorbent slurry, which is sucked into cavities of defined volume. The data generated using this device are of modeling quality as was shown for multi-component isotherms of lysozyme and cytochrome c [110]. Muthukumar and Rathore [111] presented an MTP-based membrane chromatography approach using AcroPrep Advance 96-well filter plates of 7 μL membrane volume (Pall Corp.) for the Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor, which is an alternative approach to chromatography based on adsorptive beads. A different system for batch-binding experiments was commercialized by PhyNexus. Analogous experiments as in filter plates can be realized by simple aspirating and dispensing steps using adsorbent-packed pipetting tips. Binding, washing, and elution buffers can easily be tested with standard pipetting equipment. The PhyNexus tips are commonly used for fast isolation steps such as affinity chromatography of Fab fragments [112]. Prater et al. applied the system as a crude mixture clearance step for glycoprotein mapping [113]. Whereas batch-binding experiments can be a good start for investigating biomolecule-adsorbent interactions, the industrially relevant dynamic binding setups in chromatography columns are much more complex. Industrial setups are performed far from the thermodynamic-binding equilibrium with chromatography column contact times being in a range of several minutes only. For generating dynamic binding data in small-scale and mimicking large-scale industrially relevant setups, different small-scale columns were introduced. Miniaturized columns of milliliter scale for LC systems are, e.g. MediaScout MiniChrom columns (Atoll) as used for purification of mAbs and bovine β-lactoglobulin [114,115] and HiTrap Columns (GE Healthcare Life Sciences) as applied for recombinant HIV-1 capsid purification [116]. A further reduction in column size and volume in combination with the possibility to implement column chromatography into the robotic work flow was realized with the MediaScout RoboColumn technology (Atoll) [117]. The 200-600 μL columns are not connected to tubings as in traditional LC systems and are placed in a fixing device on the robotic work station. The loading of the columns is performed by application of the liquid handling pipettor into the conically shaped column inlet. Application of different buffers and salt steps requires the aspiration of new liquids from a reservoir, which makes this chromatography technology rather semi-continuous. The sample collection is realized by catching the droplets leaving the columns in MTPs resulting in a chromatogram resolution dependent on droplet and fraction size. Nowadays, RoboColumns are widely applied in academic research as well as in industry as effective scale down models. Their validity was proven in multi-stage mAb processes [118,119], BSA, and lipolase [117], as well as antibody fragment purification [39]. Atoll expanded the product pipeline of RoboColumns on miniaturized columns of 0.05-0.6 mL bed volume, which can be operated without the need of a robotic system. One of these systems allows for liquid flow by manual pipetting (PipetColumns), the other by centrifugal force (CentriColumns) [120]. AcroSep Columns (Pall Corp.) are another straight-to-use column chromatography system without the need of robotic or LC equipment used for the purification of mAbs from hybridoma clones [121]. The columns are equipped with a Luer lock system enabling a direct connection to syringes for liquid flow.

## Modeling Approaches

Gaining a more profound understanding of biopharmaceutical USP and DSP is a key demand of the Quality by Design guideline. Where heuristic knowledge and trial and error HT technologies describe a good foundation for process understanding, modeling evolves as a central tool in process development [122]. Modeling and simulations can drastically reduce the number of experiments while enhancing or capturing the experimental content [122]. Models are generally divided into two categories: empirical and mechanistic models. Empirical models are based on a priori known output data (e.g. certain results from HT experiments) within a defined design space. The created model then allows for predictions for unknown experiments within the calibrated or extrapolated region without mechanistic or biochemical foundation of the model parameters. By contrast, mechanistic models are based on physicochemical properties and rely on calibration experiments for the determination of model and property parameters. Osberghaus et al. [123] compared both types of models in an IEX chromatography case study for the separation of lysozyme, ribonuclease a, and cytochrome c revealing the limitations of simple empirical models.

### Response Surface Modeling

RSM is one example of empirical modeling that fits a regression function for experimental results collected under defined conditions without the knowledge of the physicochemical background of the estimated parameters [124]. Generally, linear or quadratic response surface models are widely used for IEX chromatography, whereas models of higher order are known to be more and more error-prone [123]. RSM is common practice in Design of Experiments (DoE) programs such as Modde (Umetrics), Design-Expert (Stat-Ease Inc.), Fusion Pro (S- Matrix Corporation), or the JMP software (SAS Institute), which is widely applied in pharmaceutical industry for investigating the influence and interference of different parameters such as pH, ionic strength, etc. on different quality attributes [125]. DoE- RSM is employed at all stages of biopharmaceutical production: In USP applications, laccase production in Panus tigrinus cultures was modeled with respect to the impact of parameters like glucose and nitrogen concentration and three different inducers [126]. Islam et al. [127] created an RSM model on soluble recombinant protein production in MTP format using E. coli under different media, growth, induction, and aeration conditions yielding in a three-fold increase in firefly luciferase concentration. In DSP applications, DoE-RSM was used for designing an alternative mAb mixed-mode chromatography purification step including variation in chromatography media, pH, and conductivity [128]. A detailed discussion on bioprocess optimization strategies based on empirical models was reviewed by Mandenius and Brundin [124].

### Multivariate Calibration Modeling

RSM is regarded as black box modeling, which is why the trends discovered can be error-prone and misleading. Also, data generated in a biopharmaceutical process or derived from computational simulations are often so complex and multitudinous that RSM fails to find truly predictive models. Multivariate calibration modeling (MCM) describes an efficient way to analyze multi-dimensional datasets using projection methods such as principal component analysis and projection to latent structures [129]. Complex datasets can then be condensed to the factors of highest information content. Based on training sets, the multivariate calibration models can be calibrated and validated using cross-validation or internal test sets [130]. The application of MCM in biopharmaceutical manufacturing is diverse. Currently, it is used for the collection of real-time process information in terms of multivariate data analysis of spectra. Vaidyanathan et al. [131] used near-infrared spectral data for investigating complex feedstocks from an antibiotic production process. Deconvolution of protein spectra in the mid- UV region was shown to be highly useful in determining protein concentrations from multi-component mixtures [132-134]. Brestrich et al. [135] expanded the application of such a methodology to industrial process steps including in-line quantification of higher and lower molecular weight species during mAb polishing and of serum proteins during the purification of Cohn supernatant. Principal component analysis of mid-UV protein spectra was also employed for investigating conformational stability of lysozyme under high-salt HIC conditions [39]. Diverse applications of MCM used in biomedical analysis were reviewed by Escandar et al. [136]. Xu and Glatz [137] used projection to latent structures for correlating the pI, molecular weight, and the aqueous two-phase partitioning coefficients of different proteins to their retention behavior on IEX chromatography media. Another hot topic in biopharmaceutical research is the combination of MCM and molecular dynamics simulations called quantitative structure-property (QSPR) or structure-activity relationship (QSAR). Starting from in silico three-dimensional molecule structures under defined chemical conditions, different property and structure descriptors such as hydrophobicity, charge distribution, and size are extracted into a data bank [9]. Experiments performed under defined conditions then serve as a training set for correlating the most influential molecular descriptors to certain molecule properties or activities. The selection and collinear linkage of the descriptors is based on MCM as discussed above. The validated QSAR or QSPR models can then be applied for extrapolation and predicting the behavior of new molecules or process conditions. Yang et al. [138] used QSPR for characterizing multi-modal IEX ligands with respect to protein binding under high-salt conditions, as demonstrated for the model proteins RNase A, cytochrome c, and lysozyme. Schaller et al. [139] used the three-dimensional structure of proteins for the prediction of soluble peptide surfactant DAMP4 variant expression in E. coli. In a study by Asadollahi-Baboli and Mani- Varnosfaderani [140], different thiazolidine-4-carboxylic acid derivates were investigated in terms of influenza virus neuramidase inhibitor activity and correlated to the respective molecule structure in a QSAR approach. Dismer et al. [141] used molecular descriptors such as the relative hydrophobicity of PEG molecules to predict phase separations and even partitioning coefficients for lysozyme as a model protein. MCM can thus be a link between empiric and purely mechanistic modeling and the validity of the models relies on the choice of calibration experiments and the correct data handling.

### Mechanistic Modeling

Whereas empiric models as in RSM simply describe the ultimate outcome of a process under defined conditions (black box model), mechanistic models are based on a fundamental understanding of the underlying mechanisms resulting in the observed results. Mechanistic models thus need to include physicochemical properties of different interacting species to describe the final outcome. Such models are mostly of the convection diffusion reaction type describing hydrodynamics (e.g. equations of continuity, mass balances), mass transfer (e.g. film diffusion), and interaction (e.g. protein-protein, protein-ligand). In a simplified case of batch thermodynamic equilibrium, a mechanistic model can be of the reaction type only. Andrews and Roberts [142] described protein phase transitions such as non-native protein aggregation in the Lumry-Eyring Nucleation-Polymerisation model. The thermodynamic model includes reversible conformational changes of the monomers, reversible non-native oligomer formation, as well as irreversible conformational changes during nucleation and aggregate growth. Also, thermodynamic models for protein-ligand interactions as used in chromatography are widely applied in pharmaceutical industry and research. Limousin et al. [143] reviewed different adsorption isotherms, which are commonly used depending on the complexity of the protein-binding process. The list of binding isotherms includes models such as linear, Freundlich, Temkin, and Langmuir in different combinations as well as in single-component and multi-component format. Foo and Hameed [144] extended the list of binding isotherms including models such as the BET isotherm, which accounts for multilayer binding after coverage of the adsorbent surface. The common single-component Langmuir isotherm depends on two estimation parameters only, being the equilibrium-binding coefficient Keq and the maximum binding capacity qmax. When assuming multi-layer adsorption as for the BET isotherm, an additional solute solubility factor csat is included. The complexity of sorption models can be increased steadily, whereas the number of parameters to be estimated rises accordingly and might result in over-fitting. Different attributes included in multiple isotherms such as linear and non-linear adsorption, salt ion dependence, and induced salt gradients upon binding are discussed by Iyer et al. [145]. The semi-mechanistic steric mass-action isotherm introduced by Brooks and Cramer [146] as an adsorption model for IEX chromatography includes factors for varying salt concentrations, counter-ion displacement upon protein binding, as well as characteristic protein properties such as the characteristic charge and steric shielding. The steric mass-action model was applied for the AEX binding of rotavirus-like particles [147], and the separation of mAb monomers and dimers [145]. Sellberg et al. [148] used a reaction model that combined both, a chromatography model for mAb binding behavior and a coupled model for product dimer formation. When moving from pure reaction models to kinetic models including hydrodynamics and mass transfer phenomena (convection diffusion reaction type), different modes of operation can be chosen while keeping the model as simple as possible and as detailed as needed [149]. In experimental setups of high mass transfer resistance, the general rate model (GRM) is a suitable option. It covers fluid convection, axial dispersion of the fluid, as well as internal and external mass transport phenomena [150]. The GRM was employed for modeling the IEX separation of BSA and IgG [151] as well as for extracting B19 parvovirus-like particles from an Sf9 insect cell broth using a hydrogel-crafted AEX membrane [152]. The transport-dispersive model is a simplification of the GRM as film and pore diffusion is combined in a lumped effective mass transfer coefficient. It is commonly used for modeling standard column chromatography procedures. Such a setup was employed for the AEX separation of a liver phase-2 enzyme produced in E. coli [153] and modeling of an antibody platform process [148]. Another lumped-rate model including convection, dispersion, and adsorption kinetics is the reactive dispersive model [154]. A further reduction in complexity yields in a model such as the equilibrium dispersive model (EDM), which only accounts for convection and axial dispersion, while neglecting internal and external mass transfer. Close et al. [155] used an EDM for optimizing operating conditions of an HIC setup to purify a therapeutic protein from a crude feed stream. The reduction in model complexity resulted in drastically reduced calculation times while assuring the identification of critical quality attributes. A simplification of the EDM results in the ideal model that excludes axial dispersion effects and only accounts for convection [154]. Different in silico optimization studies can be found in the literature including separation of small molecules [156], model proteins [123], mAbs [157, 158], as well as industrial process applications [159,160]. Besides, custom-designed tools for modeling also commercially available solutions exist, making in silico tools accessible for a broader public. Such programs include Aspen Chromatography (AspenTech) [161], CADET (Forschungszentrum Jülich) [162], Chromulator (Ohio University) [163], ChromWorks (Ypso-Facto) [164], and ChromX (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology) [165].

## Combinatorial Approaches

Approaches based on heuristics, HT experimentation, and modeling alone constitute a good basis for fast and effective process development, but their full potential can only be realized in a combination of these above-mentioned procedures in so-called combinatorial approaches. Such a combination of approaches can be in terms of multi-stage or superstructure optimizations of consecutive unit operations, or in terms of complex feedstock characterization for tailored process development. The latter can either be realized experimentally (deterministic approach) or in silico (hybrid approach) as illustrated in Fig. 2. A large number of lysates generated in miniaturized cultivations under varying growth conditions (blue box) can be analyzed in terms of critical impurities (CIs) either experimentally (red box) or using computational methods (yellow box) for fast and dedicated downstream process development. CIs are generally regarded as molecules of similar or identical physicochemical properties as the product. Feasible lysates from product cultivation are analyzed with respect to their impurity profiles resulting in an integrated evaluation of USP and DSP performance (Fig. 2, center). Feasible process conditions can then either be used as an optimized process or experimentally refined by further exploration of the design space.

### Multi-Stage/Superstructure Process Development

Multi-stage or superstructure process optimization does not aim at optimizing single unit operations but at finding an ideal combination of consecutive steps. As the number of variables increases exponentially with the number of possible process stages, such approaches can hardly be realized experimentally. Computational approaches have the highest potential for performing a maximum number of in silico experiments. Samsatli and

**Figure 2. Schematic illustration of an integrated biopharmaceutical process development for up- and downstream applications based on combinatorial approaches. A large set of feasible complex feedstocks from micro-scale cultivations are characterized in terms of critical impurities. The characterization can be performed experimentally (deterministic approach-red box) or in silico (hybrid approach-yellow box).**

Shah [166] presented an integrated design for biochemical processes by a two-stage optimization. The first stage represents the dynamic phase for the optimization of volume handling, operational constraints, processing times, and the number of maximum unit operations. The second stage then accounts for time schedules and total consecutive process design [167]. Asenjo et al. [168] proposed a strategy for designing a batch protein plant in a modular structure using process performance models and keeping plant structure as well as process variables flexible. Vásquez-Alvarez and Pinto [169] presented mixed integer linear programming models for designing consecutive chromatography process development. Each specific chromatography model includes physicochemical properties of the molecule pool and possible purification routes to guarantee economic processes. In a case study by Huuk et al. [170], a purification procedure for two consecutive IEX steps was optimized in an integrated manner for a three-component mixture of proteins. The study was performed by in silico modeling of both setups in all possible combinations while the output pool of the first column served as the input signal of the following step. Zhou and Titchener-Hooker [171, 172] presented the technology of integrated bioprocess design based on operation windows and multi-objective Pareto optimization. The sweet spots of different unit operations can be analyzed graphically to make decisions on feasible combinations as shown for an integrated optimization of cell homogenization and debris removal of an intracellular Saccharomyces cerevisiae enzyme process.

### Deterministic Approach

The deterministic approach is a combination of the experimental and the heuristic approach. Well-chosen screening experiments serve for determination of the key parameters of certain processes and complex lysate characterization. For IEX chromatography, pH gradient chromatography was proposed as a tool for identifying CIs with similar elution conditions as the product. Ahamed et al. [173] investigated the elution behavior of 17 model proteins including related species such as isoforms in terms of elution pH and nominal pI from the literature. Kröner et al. [32] performed a multi-dimensional analysis for the isolation of Nucleolin from Sf9 feedstocks starting a pre-fractionation using pH gradients. In a study by Baumann et al. [7], pH gradients served as a systematic screening tool for IEX process development and lysate characterization including salt-intolerant proteins as demonstrated for human α-Galactosidase A from a complex Pichia pastoris supernatant. For HIC, such a characterization based on pH gradients is hard to accomplish. However, the central parameter as an analogue to the elution pH in IEX was identified as the protein solubility [39]. Conditions of decreased solubility result in an increase in HIC binding. As a consequence, CIs in HIC are supposedly molecules of similar phase behavior as the product.

### Hybrid Approach

The hybrid approach can be seen as a link between experimental process development and modeling. The determination of key parameters and CIs for complex lysate characterization is performed in silico. As mechanistic models allow for modeling of the product as well as lumped impurity peaks in different chromatography setups, even peaks overlapping with the product can be identified. Cell lysates from different cultivation conditions can thus be analyzed in silico using computational sampling of all possible fractionation setups followed by multi-objective characterization. Baumann et al. [47] used such a setup for an integrated USP and DSP optimization for a phase II liver enzyme from E. coli. It was shown that the overall optimal system must not be the upstream condition of highest initial product titer. Hanke and Ottens [9] reviewed different setups that can be used in hybrid approaches in terms of HT data generation and in silico predictions such as molecular properties (QSPR, QSAR, molecular dynamics) and model parameters such as isotherm data. Such properties include molecular mass, conformation, diffusivity, net charge, hydrophobicity, solubility, interaction coefficients, and many others.

## Concluding Remarks

With the biopharmaceutical industry going besides large-quantity productions such as antibody platform processes to personalized or precision medicine, new fast and effective processes need to be developed within a short time frame. The Quality by Design guideline stated by the authorities demands a deeper process understanding, which is why traditional heuristics alone are no longer accepted. The implementation and commercialization of HT and mechanistic modeling tools at almost all stages of biopharmaceutical productions have opened up an entirely new playground for process development. This overview summarizes the pillars of process development of heuristic, experimental, or model-based nature. It is shown how simple heuristics can help find suitable initial datasets for experimental exploration of the design space and how experimental data can inversely result in new platform processes. Also, with mechanistic models becoming the gold standard in the biopharmaceutical industry, the experimental approach will always be needed for model calibration and validation purposes. Finally, the synergetic power of combinatorial approaches is shown in deterministic and hybrid approaches. Experimental or in silico lysate characterization enables up- and downstream optimization in an entirely integrated fashion. With such new tools, it will now be possible to react on changes in the biopharmaceutical workflow. This will be especially important for continuous processing setups, which are subject to changes in the feed stream over the production time.

# Hybrid Modeling for Bioprocesses: Architectures, Applications, and Perspectives

DOI: `10.1002/eng2.70502`

Juan Federico Herrera-Ruiz | Javier Fontalvo | Oscar Andrés Prado-Rubio

**Keywords:** bioprocesses engineering | hybrid modeling | semi-parametric modeling, modeling

## Abstract

Recent hardware developments within industrial digitalization make more evident the need of high-fidelity models to exploit process system engineering potential in biomanufacturing. Hybrid models, which combine first-principles (white-box) and data-driven (black-box) approaches, aim to leverage the strengths of both methodologies to mitigate their individual limitations to provide high predictive power. This article explores the integration of hybrid modeling techniques in bioprocess engineering, emphasizing their potential to facilitate product development, accelerate experimental design, enhance process monitoring, drive optimization and catalyze the implementation of digitalization strategies to achieve a more robust and sustainable production in the framework of the goals set by the UN 2030 agenda. In this review, we analyze 270 publications from the early 1990s to 2024, extracting application domains, hybrid-model architectures, implementation software, and nonparametric output structures. Our findings highlight marked improvements in predictive accuracy, and extrapolation capabilities while revealing persistent challenges in integrating mechanistic and empirical components. This review on hybrid modeling implementations shows their potential to enhance accuracy, calibration, and extrapolation capabilities, highly required for bioprocesses. This work underscores the importance of integrating mechanistic and data-driven approaches to improve the flexibility and interpretability of models in complex engineering systems, offering significant implications for more sustainable and innovative bioprocesses.

## 1. Introduction

Sustainability has become a critical focus in addressing global challenges, as it ensures that current development meets the needs of present generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), set by the United Nations, provide a comprehensive framework to tackle pressing issues such as climate change and environmental degradation. Among these, goals like Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure (SDG9), Responsible Consumption and Production (SDG 12), Climate Action (SDG 13), and Life Below Water (SDG 14) are directly impacted by how industries operate, making sustainable practices essential [1]. As of 2024, the SDGs were in a dire situation, with most of them being severely delayed and targets not on track to being met [1]. For SDG 9, less than 20% of the targets were on track to being met, whereas for SDG 12 the share was around 30%. Moreover, the UN estimates that 84% of the SDG targets have either stagnated or shown a reversal of progress. This indicates that further acceleration is needed to achieve the targets. Research in diverse

areas of knowledge and articulation with industry is crucial to meet the 2030 agenda [1]. In the framework of the above-mentioned goals, biorefineries emerge as an attractive approach to achieve them. Second and third generation biorefineries (2G and 3G) allow biomass and agricultural wastes to take full potential, without compromising food security, which in turn makes them very attractive for adding value to waste [2]. Bioprocesses offer a promising avenue to meet sustainability goals by reducing reliance on fossil fuels and lowering carbon footprints [3]. However, they also pose significant challenges, including the complexity of biological systems and the need to balance economic viability with ecological responsibility [4]. Moreover, biorefineries are often complex processes that involve many steps, posing a technical challenge from their inception through the implementation. One of the main challenges of biorefineries takes place in the bioreaction stage. Biotransformations are intricate, and their mechanisms are usually not well understood, which leads to low titer, productivity, and yield. Process systems engineering (PSE) plays a vital role in addressing these challenges by integrating knowledge from engineering, mathematics, and computer science to optimize bioprocesses [5]. PSE methods enable the design, control, and operation of bioprocess systems in a way that improves efficiency and minimizes environmental impact. For instance, through advanced modeling, simulation, and optimization techniques, PSE can help predict the behavior of biological systems, optimize resource usage, and identify bottlenecks in production [6, 7]. In PSE, modeling takes a central role for process simulation and its use [8, 9]. Models can administrate information from two main perspectives: structural (our understanding of the underlying mechanisms) and the model parametrization (the nature of the numeric techniques used to describe the relationships between data). From the structural point of view, first-principles, mechanistic or phenomenological models represent a wide class of models, usually called white-box, due to being developed primarily on conservation equations and physical laws. First principles models are constructed through deductive reasoning, wherein the model equations are derived from existing knowledge of the system, using established relationships such as conservation laws. Mechanistic models usually comprise a system of differential algebraic equations (DAEs). An important characteristic of mechanistic models is that they can be extrapolated to process conditions outside of the calibration space, thanks in part to being developed from conservation laws, although this is not always the case [10]. In contrast, data-driven models typically employ an inductive approach, wherein a generic mathematical model is fitted to map inputs to outputs, without considering the intrinsic structure of the phenomena, unlike their white-box counterparts [10–12]. Data-driven techniques usually take the form of arbitrary functions to model the relations between inputs and outputs. Gray models usually fall in between, combining mechanistic knowledge and data-driven techniques [13, 14]. From another perspective, models can be classified regarding the form of model parametrization. Parametric models are established beforehand based on the knowledge of the process [15]. These models possess a finite number of parameters, often characterized by physical significance, which vary according to the model’s complexity [11]. In contrast, nonparametric models are solely derived from data, lacking predefined parameters [15]. The term “nonparametric” does not mean that the model is built without parameters, but that the number of them is variable, not fixed in advance by knowledge, and that they commonly lack physical significance [11]. In nonparametric modeling, mathematical techniques such as algebraic, series expansions, machine learning (ML), and other black-box approaches are used to derive insights from inputs to outputs. These techniques are also called “surrogate models” when they are used to approximate the behavior of more complex and computationally costly models [16] and are used to describe the relevant process behavior exclusively from model-generated data, to perform calculations faster such as optimization [17, 18]. Typically, they have great predicting power inside the space of their calibration, but extrapolation is not advisable [19]. For a better understanding of the advantages and disadvantages of both parametric and nonparametric modeling, Table 1 shows a comparison between parametric and nonparametric modeling [20–27]. Table 1, presents advantages and limitations between parametric and nonparametric modeling [20–27]. Parametric models are built based on prior knowledge of the system, incorporating physical laws and constraints, which makes them highly interpretable and ensures their compliance with conservation laws. They have low variability, making them more robust and reliable, especially when data is scarce. Parametric models exhibit strong extrapolation capabilities, allowing them to make reasonable predictions beyond the range of the observed data. However, their reliance on predefined equations introduces a strong bias, which may lead to inaccurate predictions if the assumed structure does

**Table 1. Comparison between parametric and nonparametric modeling [20-27].**

| Aspect | Parametric modeling | Nonparametric modeling |

|---|---|---|

| Model variability | Low | High |

| Model bias | High | Low |

| Model parameter data required | High | Low |

| Mechanism understanding required | High | Low |

| Model flexibility | Medium | High |

| Explainability and interpretability | High | Low |

| Interpolation capabilities | Medium | High |

| Extrapolation capacities | Good | Bad |

| Computational training cost | Low | High |

| Risk of overfitting | Low | High |

| Compliance with conservation laws | High | Low |

not fully capture the system dynamics. Developing parametric models requires extensive domain expertise, making the process time-intensive and complex, often involving experts from multiple disciplines. Nonparametric models offer greater flexibility as they do not require prior mechanistic knowledge, making them particularly useful when the underlying system is poorly understood or difficult to describe mathematically. These models can efficiently capture complex, nonlinear relationships within data, often uncovering hidden patterns that parametric models might miss. However, their flexibility comes at a cost. Nonparametric models typically require large amounts of high-quality data for training, and their computational cost is significantly higher, particularly during the training phase. Additionally, they are prone to overfitting and overparameterization, making them less robust, and they often struggle with extrapolation beyond the observed data range. They are usually not reliable enough to extrapolate to conditions outside of their calibration space; however, they have great interpolation capabilities within it. Another critical drawback is their lack of interpretability, as they do not rely on physical constraints or conservation laws, which can make it difficult to understand the underlying mechanisms driving predictions. From previous experience, there is no ideal model, with both parametric and nonparametric models having strengths and shortcomings that not only depend on system understanding, but also on data and computational power. As a potential trade-off, the scientific community has proposed hybrid modeling, also called hybrid semi-parametric modeling, to overcome the challenges that arise from parametric and nonparametric modeling, while retaining most of their advantages. Notice that researchers do not always agree on the definition and use of the term “hybrid model.” Some authors claim to have developed hybrid models, when they combine different mechanistic and empiric knowledge (mathematical relationships that provide reliable approximations but are not built using mechanistic knowledge) such as correlations for heat and mass transfer coefficients, for example, [28–34]. Besides, the term has been used when modified structures apply to pure nonparametric approaches for predictions. These modifications usually entail combinations of artificial neural networks (ANNs) with other ML techniques or optimization algorithms [35–40]. Finally, “hybrid modeling” has been applied to other approaches such as Computational Fluid Dynamics applications that integrate various numerical methods [41] and process system engineering simulations that use multiple software tools to perform the simulations [42–44]. Here in, “hybrid modeling” represents a modeling paradigm that seeks to combine the strengths of both parametric and nonparametric modeling while minimizing their individual disadvantages. Hybrid modeling is an emerging approach gaining traction; thus there are recent reviews in the literature detailing the applications of hybrid modeling to separation processes [45], biochemical processes using neural networks [24, 46, 47], wastewater treatment (WTT) [48]; chemical, petroleum and energy systems [46, 49]. For bioprocesses specifically, recent reviews include topics such as the role of hybrid models in bioprocess scale-up [50]; the applications of hybrid modeling to systems biology for mammalian cell culture development [51], and the prospects of hybrid modeling for industry 4.0 and 5.0 [20, 23]. Those contributions delve into the details of relevant discussions. However, they lack quantitative and qualitative trends and information on how hybrid models have been implemented in bioprocesses. This study provides the main characteristics of hybrid models, such as structure, knowledge integration, performance assessment, data requirements, and challenges. This contribution focuses on the hybrid modeling of reactions in bioprocesses, aggregating information from 270 contributions screened down from 5890 identified from a bibliometric search. From there, the target is to identify trends such as the types of bioprocesses to which hybrid modeling has been applied, the preferred architectures/structures/design patterns, the most used nonparametric techniques, the scale of the experimental data used to develop the models, the mode of operation of the experiments, and software used for building the models, as well as cross-correlations between these categories. This study describes the literature review methodology in Section 2, Section 3 presents the general characteristics of hybrid semi-parametric models, whereas Section 4 shows insights and correlations of the different implementations of hybrid models to bioprocesses, including an overview of some recent applications of hybrid semi-parametric models to bioprocesses. Finally, Section 5 presents conclusions, current challenges, and future perspectives.

## 2. Literature Review Methodology

A comprehensive bibliometric study was performed to quantitatively and qualitatively map the research landscape using descriptors such as journals, publication outputs, institutions, authors, and keywords. Full details of the methodology for the literature review can be found elsewhere [52]. Here, a summary is presented. The search strategy began with identifying the need for information, focusing on hybrid modeling applications in bioprocesses. Non-biotechnological processes were excluded to maintain the relevance of the field. Scopus and Web of Science were selected as the primary databases due to their extensive and complementary coverage of scientific literature. A search equation was designed by expanding terms, incorporating keywords related to hybrid models (e.g., “hybrid model,” “hybrid neural network”) and bioprocesses (e.g., “bio*,” “bioproc*”). The search was restricted to publications from 1992, marking a seminal work in the field, through March 2024. The search was repeated on December 2024 to encompass new publications. Search results were refined by targeting specific fields: “Title-Abstract-Keywords” for Scopus and “Topics” for Web of Science. Abstracts were validated manually to ensure relevance to Chemical and Biochemical Engineering, excluding unrelated documents. This iterative process included refining the search equation multiple times, guided by insights gained during analysis. The search continued until results stabilized, with less than 5% variation in top authors, journals, and total results across iterations. A total of 5890 contributions were found, and after a manual review, 270 contributions were selected as of

interest. Information was refined using software like VantagePoint, VOSViewer, Bibliometrix, and Python. Later, a manual assessment of each contribution was performed.

## 3. Hybrid Modeling Framework

This section is divided into subsections to provide a clear and comprehensive look at hybrid modeling. Section 3.1 introduces the general characteristics of hybrid models, laying the groundwork for understanding their key features. Section 3.2 dives into the different structures commonly used to implement these models, whereas Section 3.3 explores various ways to incorporate knowledge into their design. Section 3.4 highlights some of the most popular nonparametric substructures used in hybrid modeling for bioprocesses. Section 3.5 focuses on how the performance of these models has been assessed, followed by Section 3.6, which discusses the data requirements necessary for building them, and lastly, Section 3.7 showcases some of the main applications of hybrid models.

### 3.1. Main Characteristics of Hybrid Modeling

In the middle of the parametric and nonparametric modeling paradigms, the called “hybrid models” or “hybrid semi-parametric models” exist, combining both first principles and data-driven techniques to describe the systems. Figure 1 shows the knowledge basis and mathematical representations for parametric, nonparametric, and hybrid modeling. Parametric models heavily rely on first principles and prior knowledge, using conservation laws, mass-energy-momentum balances, kinetic mechanisms, thermodynamic relationships, and transport laws to describe the system. Parametric models are usually expressed as algebraic equations, DAEs or partial differential equations (PDEs), with data being mostly used for parameter identification (hence the dotted green line in Figure 1). Nonparametric modeling approaches are usually data-hungry [23, 26, 45, 50] and build their knowledge exclusively from process data, extracting no information from first principles. Nonparametric models are usually expressed as data-driven techniques such as ANNs, Gaussian Processes (GPs), and support vector machines (SVMs) or Autoregressive models (ARX, ARMAX, ARIMA). Hybrid modeling aims to compromise both approaches in the middle, needing fewer data than nonparametric models, but without requiring prior knowledge as extensive as parametric models do. Hybrid models can be expressed in a wide range of structures, mixing the data-driven techniques used for nonparametric modeling and the mechanistic knowledge expressed in parametric models. It is important to note that hybrid models do not necessarily use their parametric and nonparametric components in the same ratio. Thus, the spectrum seen in Figure 1 signals that hybrid models can be “darker” if they rely more on the nonparametric techniques than the mechanistic ones, or “lighter” if the inverse is true. Literature often claims that hybrid modeling leverages most of the advantages of parametric and nonparametric modeling while minimizing its disadvantages. Although this is empirically seen in an increased performance when compared against full mechanistic models, there are sparse mathematical proofs. It has been proven that giving more structure to the nonparametric subcomponent via an additive term helps to reduce the asymptotic variance of the parametric parameters [53]. Authors prove that if the parametric model is ill conditioned, hybrid models will outperform it. Furthermore, a Focused Information Criterion is

**Figure 1.** Parametric, nonparametric, and hybrid semi-parametric modeling and the types of knowledge they are based on. Adapted from [11].

proposed, showing that in small data samples hybrid models are heavily reliant on induced bias from parametric ones, but if the data has low variance, the hybrid model enhances prediction capabilities requiring less data than a full nonparametric approach [54]. Hybrid modeling main characteristics are [25, 26, 49, 55]:

1. Hybrid models usually present better parameter estimation,

due to:

a. Less parameters than pure nonparametric techniques,

which can lead to higher statistical confidence of the identified parameters.

b. The chance to map all measurable quantities as inputs to

the model structure, where the relationships are established using the nonparametric sub model. Thus, more information is included than in parametric models, usually allowed due to deficiencies in process understanding.

c. Combining data-driven approaches with mechanistic

knowledge results in a constrained space that imposes physical meaning and bounds to the variables, which is hard to achieve in pure nonparametric techniques.

d. When compared to pure nonparametric models, hybrid

modeling exhibits superior calibration properties and enhanced extrapolation properties when compared to pure nonparametric techniques due to the structuring of the operation space using mechanistic or phenomenological knowledge. This structuring reduces the search space, consequently requiring less data for training hybrid models than for pure nonparametric approaches. However, the strategies for training and validation of hybrid models are heavily dependent on the model structure/architecture chosen.

2. Less mechanistic or first principles knowledge is needed for

developing a hybrid model than a complex pure parametric model.

3. Hybrid models are usually developed faster than pure

parametric models, since less mechanistic knowledge is required. However, they are highly dependent on quality data and its availability.

4. The mechanistic knowledge enhances the model inter-

pretability, making it more “transparent” than nonparametric models (hence the term “gray box model” is also used).

### 3.2. Hybrid Model Design Patterns

Recently, a comprehensive overview of design patterns for hybrid models was presented [26]. These design patterns generalize, unify, and formalize diverse modeling approaches across various domains and applications. The following sections introduce these patterns and illustrate them through selected relevant studies from the literature. Notice that the chemical engineering literature has used the term “architecture” [11, 23, 56]. Recently, a distinction between “design pattern” and “architecture” was proposed because any model architecture can have different combinations of different design patterns, working in parallel, in series or nested inside another [26]. In the present work, “architecture” and “design pattern” are synonyms, whereas “structure” is used to discuss the different combinations and arrangements of the design patterns. It is important to note that a model structure can comprise one or several design patterns. Agarwal [56] presented the general architectures in which the white box and black box components of a hybrid model can be arranged. Figure 2 shows three configurations. Configurations (a) and (b) show a serial architecture, where a black box output serves as input for the white box, and the white box output serves as input for the black box, respectively. Configuration (c) shows a parallel architecture, and finally, configuration (d) shows a data-driven technique constrained by a parametric model. Configurations (a), (b), (c), and (d) are also called “feature learning,” “physics-based preprocessing,” “delta model,” and “physical constraints,” respectively [26]. In Figure 2 there are two types of inputs for configurations (a), (b), and (c), named x1 and x2 (color coded blue and green, respectively) to clarify that the inputs for the different subcomponents of hybrid models might be different, but also could include common variables.

**Figure 2.** Types of design patterns used for building hybrid models: (a) feature learning; (b) physics-based preprocessing; (c) delta model; (d) physical constraints Adapted from [11, 26].

The design pattern choice not only influences the interaction between the different components of a hybrid model, but also determines the training strategy and, therefore, computational cost of developing a model.

#### 3.2.1. Serial Architectures

The most popular hybrid model architecture is the “feature learning” design pattern. In this architecture, the white box is usually composed of conservation laws, mass, heat, or momentum transfer relations that describe the process. The black box typically represents the kinetics of the process or the transport coefficients, for which there is no general valid model [10, 47, 57]. This architecture is very useful when there is no precise knowledge of the underlying mechanisms, but there is enough data to identify the underlying patterns. Another scenario is presented when there is a huge amount of data that can be exploited to model the underlying mechanisms [58, 59]. The “physics-based preprocessing” design pattern is mostly used in data sparse environments, primarily using data augmentation [12]. In this architecture, the white-box model predictions are used to establish a link between the state of the system and certain parameters [11]. Some examples include: the prediction of cell culture using ANNs [60] where authors used an ANN to model some reaction rates in their dynamic balance flux model using other mechanistic reaction rates and states and inputs to the data-driven components, a fed-batch process for producing penicillin [61] taking advantage of Kalman filters to estimate and reconstruct some states from noisy data and predict fault detections, the control of biomass in protein production using Pichia pastoris [62] implementing a soft-sensor to predict biomass concentration based on online measurements of CO2 utilizing a multi-linear regression that takes advantage of the mechanistic carbon balance. When utilizing serial architectures, the training can be done in two different ways: coupling the identification of the parametric and nonparametric components simultaneously or decoupling the identification, usually calibrating a parametric structure and then calibrating a nonparametric component to account for the deficiencies of the parametric component.

#### 3.2.2. Parallel Architecture

The parallel architecture (“delta model” design pattern) applies if there is a process model (white box) that captures the underlying mechanisms but has limited predictive power due to structural factors not accounted for (unmodeled effects, nonlinearities, dynamic behavior) [26]. The predictive power of the model can be enhanced using nonparametric techniques, although their performance remains poor outside of the training region [11, 23]. This structure is interesting if the system can be decoupled into non-interacting parts, that is, static non-linear and dynamic linear behavior. This modeling approach has been applied to cases such as predicting phosphorus removal in a WTT process [63] correcting the model’s mismatch by adding the output of an ANN to the mechanistic reaction rates to enhance prediction capabilities; using Kalman filters to correct bias from mechanistic model predictions and enabling higher forecasting capabilities in each integration time in ethanol fermentations for biofuel production [64]; using ANNs to correct the predictions of parametric models in cell apoptosis [65]; applying corrections to the activated sludge model in an industrial cokes wastewater-plant [66] correcting the activated sludge model by using five different data-driven techniques like ANNs and multiple linear regressions; predicting biomass concentration in a baker’s yeast fermentation [67] utilizing a mixture of experts, where each data-driven component is used to predict the states and a gating function combines them for enhancing prediction capabilities; studying polymerization processes by simplifying the parametric structure of the model [68] or fed-batch penicillin fermentations [15] where simplified models are proposed and the data-driven techniques take full advantage of residuals and state predictions to have similar performance to more computationally demanding models. Researchers have proposed three main ways for approaching the parallel structure, shown in Figure 3 [11]. The (a) configuration is called “superposition” where the black box output is summed or subtracted from the white box model prediction to enhance the model performance. This configuration works as a bias correction, changing the output variance and shape. This is the most used parallel structure, first proposed in bioprocesses to study a fed-batch penicillin fermentation [15]. Configuration (b) is called “multiplication” because the output of the model is the multiplication of the outputs predicted by the black box and white box, working as a correction factor (amplification or mitigation of the parametric outputs). It was first utilized in bioprocesses for a bakers’ yeast production process [17]. The (c) configuration is applied when the outputs of the black box and white box are transformed by either a black box or a white box model [69], as such, weight factors (w1 and w2) are applied to combine them and obtain the final prediction. It is important to note that the inputs to the nonparametric and parametric parts could be different (as evidenced in Figure 3); therefore, the nonparametric component might obtain knowledge from information that the parametric models do not consider in their formulation.

#### 3.2.3. Physical Constraints

Physical constraints represent a hybrid modeling design pattern that integrates domain knowledge—such as conservation laws—into the structure, parameters, or outputs of a data-driven model [20, 26, 70]. These constraints can be categorized as hard constraints and soft constraints, based on how strictly they are enforced.

- Hard constraints encode physical principles directly into

the model’s structure, ensuring they are never violated. For instance, adding a ReLU (rectified linear unit function, which is a function that is 0 when its input is less than or equal to 0 and is a linear function when its input is greater than 0) activation layer to guarantee non-negative outputs for variables like concentrations or pressure, or using a softmax layer to ensure molar fractions sum to one, are common examples [71]; or using Neural ODEs to predict ethanol production via fermentation [72] or Chinese Hamster Ovary cells (CHO) biomass growth in a bioreactor [73]. However, hard constraints require the input data to align with the

**Figure 3.** Types of design pattern architecture. (a) linear superposition; (b) multiplication; (c) weighed predictions by using either a black box or a white box. The individual predictions of white boxes are denoted as b(x2) while for black boxes they are denoted as a(x1). In configuration (c), the individual predictions are added using weighting factors (w1 and w2). Adapted from [11].

imposed rules, a process known as data reconciliation [20]. A challenge with hard constraints is that they can result in non-differentiable models complicating gradient-based optimization methods [26].

- Soft constraints incorporate mechanistic insights into the

loss function as penalties. These penalties guide the model during training to produce outputs that align with domain knowledge, allowing some flexibility in how strictly the constraints are followed [20, 26]. Once training is complete, the model relies solely on the data-driven architecture, with the domain knowledge encoded implicitly. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are an example of soft-constrained models [70]. PINNs have been successfully applied to simulated cases of bioprocesses [74, 75]; kinetics of biodiesel production [76]; and WTT plants [75]. When using hard constraints at the output, the results are guaranteed to be physically plausible; however, these constraints can introduce non-differentiable nonlinearities that complicate gradient-based optimization. To address this, soft constraints are sometimes used because they provide a smoother optimization landscape, even though they do not guarantee exact adherence to the desired conditions. Moreover, combining multiple physical constraints in a single model can be challenging. A key benefit of incorporating physical constraints is enhanced data efficiency. By embedding prior knowledge into the model, the complexity of the problem can be reduced, which in turn lowers the amount of training data needed [26].

### 3.3. Knowledge Integration

The standard way to incorporate mechanistic knowledge into a hybrid model is using mathematical expressions such as conservation laws or underlying phenomena. But they are not the only form of knowledge that can be incorporated. Some examples are:

- Knowledge about different stages of a process (e.g., growth

phase; lag phase; etc. for a fermentation) can be leveraged to apply fuzzy logic (FL) either to enhance prediction for each phase by changing the mechanistic model [77–80] or to change the structure of ANNs [81].

- Design of experiments can evaluate and optimize the black

box structure [82].

- Constraints can be added to the output predictions of the

hybrid model to enhance its performance [25].

- Physics laws can be encoded in the training phase of the

black-box component as in Physics Informed Neural Networks [47]. Mechanistic knowledge should be incorporated only if it is highly certain, which means that it does not contain empirical assumptions to avoid producing a model with high bias. The white box should be limited to knowledge that represents the physical interactions of the system [25]. For example, mass balances can be incorporated without hesitation, as the mass conservation laws apply to all systems. Assumptions like lumped parameters in a

chemostat might not always hold true, especially in large systems; therefore, the assumption introduces bias to the model. The unknown elements of a hybrid model, such as kinetic terms, unknown or unmeasured variables, or mass transfer coefficients are usually represented by a nonparametric structure.

### 3.4. Data Driven Components of Hybrid Models

Since the beginning of the century, the increasing availability of data, driven by the continuous advancement of better and more precise sensors, larger databases, and enhanced computational power, has compelled engineers to recognize data as a valuable source of information [12]. Therefore, mathematical techniques that build insights from data are highly valuable. Non-parametric and data-driven techniques can be broadly classified in the following categories, with accompanying examples of their applications to bioprocesses:

- Algebraic expressions such as polynomials or rational func-

tions for predicting the pH and acetic acid production of Kombucha fermentations [83], and sigmoidal and exponential functions for describing methane production during the anaerobic digestion of orange peel waste [84].

- Series expressions such as Fourier series used for optimizing

the pH profile for controlling the process of the yeast Wickerhamomyces anomalus against the spoilage yeast Zygosaccharomyces rouxii in wine pre-fermentation [85].

- Statistical models such as principal component analysis

(PCA) for identifying the correlations between variables for monoclonal antibodies production [86], and multivariate data analysis (MVDA) for predicting the production of adenovirus using human embryonic kidney cells (HEK 293) [87].

- Time-series autoregressive approaches such as ARMAX for

controlling dissolved oxygen in a S. cerevisiae fermentation [88], ARIMA for modeling and predicting a membrane bioreactor (MBR) for treating ampicillin from pharmaceutical wastewater [89] or ARX for predicting biomass concentrations in a lactic acid fermentation [90].

- ML approaches such as ANNs, as well as techniques like

GPs or SVMs [91]. An overview of several nonparametric structures such as ANNs, Random Forests (RF), SVMs, GPs, among others has been recently presented [92]. The choice of nonparametric technique coupled with the hybrid model’s structure heavily influences the development and the strategy for training and validation of the model.

### 3.5. Hybrid Model Performance Assessment

Hybrid models’ performance and extrapolation capabilities are directly related to the structure of the nonparametric portion of the model. This refers not only to whether the architecture is parallel or serial but also to the configuration and the specific model structure of the nonparametric model, particularly its size (e.g., layers of an ANN, number of neurons per layer, type of activation function, etc.) [11]. The size of the data-driven technique can be assessed using the Akaike Information Criteria (AIC) or Bayesian Information Criteria (BIC), the latter being preferred for models with a high number of parameters [55, 57]. For discriminating between models, Friedman’s test can be applied [93]. In general, there should be a trade-off between estimation quality and the number of parameters, to avoid overfitting or underfitting issues, which should also be addressed in training and validation. To compare hybrid models’ performance to traditional parametric and nonparametric models, researchers have also used more conventional metrics such as the coefficient of determination r2 despite not being suited for nonlinear estimators in biochemical systems [94], the mean squared error (MSE) and its derivatives such as root mean square error (RMSE) or normalized MSE (NMSE), error measurements such as mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), mean absolute error (MAE), among others. When extrapolating the hybrid model’s predictions outside the training domain, some assessment of the validity of the extrapolation should be done. Authors have mainly used two complementary criteria: convex-hull criteria and a confidence interval criterion. The convex-hull criteria are used to verify that each empirical model solely interpolates the data gathered during model identification. Meanwhile, the confidence interval criterion evaluates the confidence intervals for the predictions of the hybrid model [95]. Other authors have proposed that the confidence interval of the hybrid model can be estimated using Bayesian optimization, resampling the model’s prediction using Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations [96].

### 3.6. Hybrid Modeling Requirements for Data

Data is essential for discerning the structure and parameters of the hybrid model, and principally all properties of the model (such as prediction quality and extrapolation capabilities) heavily rely both on the quality and quantity of the data [10, 12, 24]. Data is necessary to develop any hybrid model. If there is no previous data, it must be generated, with a systematic exploration of the design space (e.g., using Design of Experiments for a system or a benchmark model). Different techniques can be applied, such as factorial design, sequential design, optimal design, and model-based design methodologies [97]. A valuable alternative is the so-called “Intensified Design of Experiments,” where intra-experimental shifts to key parameters are performed to capture the dynamics of the process [59, 98, 99]. This methodology has been applied specifically to develop hybrid models, yielding great predictive power with a reduced number of experiments in an early stage of model development. Intensified design of experiments has been paired with hybrid models to transfer knowledge from lab scale to pilot scale in CHO cultures [100], reducing the number of experiments by as much as 50% while retaining the same levels of accuracy in monoclonal CHO line producing immunoglobulin G4 monoclonal antibody [101, 102], describing the design space with similar accuracy as a full-factorial design of experiments despite having less than 33%

of the experiments in an E. coli culture for recombinant protein production [103]. Regardless of the experimental design, data should be cleaned and properly pretreated before using it for hybrid modeling purposes. For example, small variances in feeding concentration can cause big errors in the estimation of substrate concentrations [57]. Hybrid model performance is affected by higher levels of noise, increasing the variance of the identified model parameters [104, 105]. Noise from data can be extracted using techniques such as outlier removal and signal filtering [106] or using surrogate models for data augmentation to increase model stability in predictions [23, 107, 108].

### 3.7. Hybrid Modeling Applications

A classification according to the use given to the hybrid model has been proposed, providing in-depth examples for each category [12]. Based on that classification, the main uses for hybrid modeling in bioprocesses are shown in Table 2. Besides the previous applications, hybrid models have gained momentum for the development of digital shadows and digital twins, to accelerate Industry 4.0 and digitalization in chemical processes [16, 119]. In the following sections, insights regarding hybrid modeling of bioprocesses are presented. Due to the vast number of references analyzed, only a select number of them will be included in the text as examples. The database of papers analyzed will be made available on request.

## 4. Hybrid Modeling Implementation

Recently, a comprehensive bibliometric analysis [52] spanning 360 contributions revealed that the hybrid modeling of bioprocesses is a growing research area, with an annual growth rate of 9% since its inception in 1992. Recent advancements, particularly post-2017, underscore the impact of heightened awareness surrounding artificial intelligence and the integration of next-generation ML techniques into hybrid models. Key themes driving this field include “hybrid model,” “neural networks,” and applications ranging from fermentation to biopharmaceutical manufacturing. A keyword network analysis identified three central research clusters: process control applications, computational techniques, and the broader integration of bioprocessing terminology with ML concepts. This review builds on these findings, delving into quantifying trends, innovations, and challenges in hybrid modeling for bioprocesses, setting the stage for a comprehensive examination of the current state of the field to identify trends such as the types of hybrid modeling on bioprocesses, the preferred design patterns, the most used nonparametric techniques, the scale of the experimental data for developing the models, the mode of operation of the experiments, software used for building the models, as well as
