current challenges and future potential. This section highlights selected examples to illustrate the main macro trends in the field, rather than providing a detailed account of all contributions. Section 4.1 presents an overview of the most used nonparametric substructures for hybrid models. Section 4.2 presents the types of processes that have been successfully modeled using hybrid semi-parametric approaches with the most used microorganisms in those processes. Section 4.3 presents the type, scale of the data and mode of operation of the processes used for hybrid modeling. Section 4.4 presents some computational details regarding the implementation of hybrid models, and finally Section 4.5 presents some recent trends.

### 4.1. Data-Driven Substructures Model Approaches

Figure 4 shows the distribution of the data-driven techniques used for hybrid modeling. A total of 374 different hybrid model implementations were found in the literature. It’s important to note that there are more individual implementations than works analyzed because one work can have more than one implementation. ANNs dominate as the preferred black box component in hybrid modeling, accounting for 56.2% of the total modeling approaches. Inside the ANN set, 67% of the authors that use ANNs do not specify the type of ANN they use, for example, using ANNs to develop hybrid models for CHO cultivation from shake flask cultivations and yielding similar accuracy to the mechanistic model despite using only 4 of 33 experiments for training [120], or to describe a B. subtilis fermentation to maximize the spores produced [121]. The remaining authors have used the following types: multi-layered perceptron (MLP), which are 13% of the applications and have been used to describe the reaction rates in perfusion cultures of mammalian cells, reducing the elementary fluxes modeled from 22,563 to 5 [60], or to predict a CHO cultivation process by replacing reaction rates with MLPs [122], or to model the enzymatic kinetics for producing galactooligosaccharides using β-galactosidase from Kluyveromyces lactis [123]. Deep Neural Networks (DNN) comprise 4% of the total ANN applications and have been used to describe processes such as the production of glycoproteins in a CHO culture, resulting in an error 12% lower when compared to the shallow counterparts despite an increase in computation time of 31% [124], modeling the E. coli threonine synthesis [125], or modeling real industrial fermentations with a 75% reduction in RMSE [126]. Feedforward Neural Networks (FNN) which account for 3% of the total ANN applications, have been used to predict the gas composition of a biomass gasification process [127] or to predict the insulinase

**Figure 4.** Distribution of black box models’ categories and subcategories used by authors when implementing hybrid Models in bioprocesses. Bubble size indicates number of occurrences in the database. ANN, artificial neural networks; BPNN, backpropagation neural networks; DNN, deep neural networks; FL, fuzzy logic; FNN, feedforward neural networks; GA, genetic algorithms; GAN, generative adversarial neural networks; GP, Gaussian Processes; KF, Kalman Filter; LSTM, long short-term memory neural networks; MARS, multi-adaptive regression splines; ML, machine learning techniques; MLP, multi-layered perceptron; PINNs, physics-informed neural networks; PLS, partial least squares; RA, regression analysis; RF, random forests; RL, reinforcement learning; RP, random processes; SVMs, support vector machines.

production in a fed-batch bioreactor using Kluyveromyces marxianus, where hybrid models performed up to 12% better than the parametric models [128]. Functional Link Neural Networks (FLN) comprise 3% of the ANNs subset and have been used to predict the behavior of a series of industrial ethanol fermenters considering the effects of recycling and temperature changes [129, 130]. PINNs are an emerging implementation with 2% of the total ANN uses in hybrid modeling of bioprocesses, for example, predicting β-carotene production using Saccharomyces cerevisiae and reducing MSE by 80% when compared with a traditional parametric model [131]. Backpropagation Neural Networks (BPNN) which represent 1% of the applications have been implemented to model the production of sodium gluconate in a fermentation by Aspergillus niger, with the hybrid model yielding errors up to 87% lower than the parametric mechanistic model [132], or to identify the metabolic fluxes in a recombinant Baby Hamster Kidney culture [133]. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks comprise 1% and have been used for predicting the pH of cream cheese fermentation at both lab and industrial scales [134] or for predicting the ethanol concentration in industrial fermenters aided by the use of Generative Adversarial Neural Networks (GAN), with 1% of the total uses of ANNs, for replacing missing datapoints of yeast [135]. In Figure 4, the Regression Analysis (RA) category refers to regression techniques that are not random processes nor ML nor ANNs, such as series expansions, polynomial expressions or time-series models like ARMAX. This category is the second biggest approach, with 16% of all the applications having a vast array of techniques at their disposal. In this category, Partial Least Squares (PLS) is the most used technique (36% of the occurrences) and has been used to describe the formation of recombinant products reducing errors by as much as three orders of magnitude when compared to traditional metabolic flux analysis [136], or to describe the mass transfer coefficient in a MBR for WTT, reducing the RMSE by 52% [137]. Linear techniques follow with 32% of the applications in this subcategory. This subcategory refers to techniques such as multivariate curve resolution coupled with mass conservation equations to describe CHO cell cultivation processes [100, 138]. Also, polynomial approaches for describing lutein production by microalgae have errors up to 5% lower than the mechanistic approach [139]. “Non-linear” refers to various techniques used in bioprocess modeling to improve predictive accuracy. One example is non-linear PLS, which has been applied to predict concentrations based on spectral data, yielding lower errors than traditional chemometric tools [140]. Another application involves modeling the specific reaction rates of a Bordetella pertussis culture by integrating both online and offline measurements, enhancing process understanding and control [112]. Similarly, multi-adaptive regression splines (MARS) have been employed in a simulated penicillin fermentation process, demonstrating superior predictive performance with mean errors 15 times lower than the parametric approach [141]. ML techniques comprise 15% of the applications. SVMs account for 47% of the applications in this subcategory and have been used in fluxomic for identifying genes to overexpress and other genes to suppress resulting in an enhanced ethanol production by 10% [142], or to optimize a nosiheptide fed-batch fermentation increasing yields by as much as 26.8% [143] or used to predict the mycelial concentration in a penicillin fermentation [144]. Reinforcement Learning (RL) accounts for 16% of the applications in this subcategory, having been used to enhance the yield prediction in a Yarrowia lipolytica fermentation process [145]. Other ML applications used are Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) for predicting viable cell density and glucose consumption in a CHO culture [146] or for predicting the rate constants in the reaction between alkyl esters and hydrogen atoms in biodiesel combustion processes [147]. Random Processes (RP) comprise 7.1% of the hybrid model’s applications, with examples such as GPs that account for 42% of this subcategory and have been used to predict the effluent composition of a full-scale WWT plant [148], or to predict an astaxanthin production system reducing MAPE by two orders of magnitude [149]. RF that comprise 18% of this subcategory have been used for predicting the production of a therapeutic protein in a CHO culture [146] or to predict the chemical oxygen demand and nitrate concentrations in a WTT plant with errors 8% lower than traditional activated sludge models [150]. The “Other” category accounts for 6% of the applications, mostly composed of Kalman Filter (KF) which is 32% of this subcategory and has been applied to reconstruct the experimental data from an E. coli fermentation [151], or to predict neuron activity in mammalian cells [152]. FL comprises 25% of the applications in this subcategory and has been used to predict the different stages of a fermentation thus adapting the model for each phase [153–155]. Genetic Algorithms (GA) are 25% of the approaches in this subcategory and have been adapted for optimizing hybrid models that describe E. coli fermentations [156, 157] or to identify and optimize the structure and parameters of chemical reaction networks [158].

### 4.2. Processes Where Hybrid Models Have Been Applied To

The type of application for which the modeling objective of the hybrid models is shown in the innermost ring of Figure 5. One hundred fifty-five different implementations were found in the literature. Most of the documents are related to Metabolite Production, processes that use hybrid models aiming to describe the concentration or behavior of a substance produced by a microorganism. The second biggest category is Cell Cultivation, where the goal of the application is to produce biomass of a microorganism. WWT is the third category, where hybrid models have been used to describe biological treatments. The “other” label accounts for processes like biosorption [159], transesterification [160], membrane separations of fermentation broths or other bio-based processes [161, 162], among others. The second ring shows how authors describe their applications. The Cell Cultivation section shows that all of them are naturally inclined to describe their processes as biomass growth. In the Metabolite Production category around half of the applications are for fermentations, followed by Protein Production and the description of Enzyme kinetics and activity of different bioprocesses, such as cellobiose using glucosidase [163], or the proteolysis of whey by alcalase [164]. In the WWT application, hybrid models have been used to describe activated sludge reactors (AS)

using synthetic data generated from benchmark models [75], ANNs for predicting reaction rates in a simulated phosphorous removal plant [165]. Besides, for WWT there are also MBRs, where the models have been used to predict biochemical oxygen demand, chemical oxygen demand, total nitrogen, and total phosphorus in a municipal WWT plant [167], suspended solids, chemical oxygen demand, and nitrite and nitrate concentration in the permeate of a MBR for WTT [109]. Also, there are applications to predict the counterion mass transfer in a membrane-supported bioreactor designed for the removal of nitrate and perchlorate from a synthetic contaminated drinking water stream [137], or to predict in real-time the phosphate concentration from municipal wastewater [168]. In “Cell Cultivation” applications, the field is dominated by CHO cells [122, 199–201] and Saccharomyces cerevisiae (displayed as “yeast” in Figure 5) [78, 131, 170, 202]. Other cases include the cultivation of Chlorella vulgaris [203], cultivation of Bacillus [204, 205]. All the different applications, with a wide margin over the different ML techniques. In Metabolite Production applications, ANNs comprise over 41% of the total applications, more than doubling all the other different black-box techniques. However, when moving to the other categories, the margin between ANNs and other types of technologies diminishes. ML techniques are the second most used black-box component overall, followed by RP, RA and other techniques. It is interesting to note that for “Metabolite Production” applications, RA is the second most used technique, but falls behind RP and ML. Other techniques are the least used, except for WWT where it becomes the second most used. One important aspect to consider is that adding the percentages of each type of application in Figure 6 does not match with the percentages given in Figure 5 due to authors exploring the use of different black-box components and combinations for their hybrid models. If a contribution uses two different black-box techniques for the same application, these are counted as separate instances (hence “double counting” some studies), which explains why “Metabolite Production” has a lower percentage and the other categories have higher percentages when compared to Figure 5. The most common architecture used is the “feature-learning” design pattern with 83% of the applications, followed by “delta model” implementations and “physics-based preprocessing” with 15% and 2% respectively (Figure 7). Some authors use a mixture of both parallel and serial architectures [144, 148, 206]. In all the design patterns, metabolite production comprises the

bulk of the applications, although inside the “delta model” implementations, the margin is thinner than in “feature learning” applications. It is important to note that Cell Cultivation processes have the same share in “feature learning” implementations than “delta model”. However, this is not the case for WWT, signaling that authors prefer “delta model” implementations when dealing with these case studies. This might be due to higher uncertainty and less mechanistic knowledge available when modeling the complex processes of WWT. Many of the WWT applications use hybrid models to predict contaminant concentrations [75, 148] or physicochemical parameters like BOD, pH, and COD [207, 208]. Regarding the outputs of the nonparametric components of hybrid models, common predictions are kinetic or transport parameters with 55% of the contributions, followed by 19% that predict reaction rates, 11% directly predict concentrations, and 15% predict other quantities such as pH, fluxes, or volumetric flows. “Delta model” architectures usually model the residuals or the mismatch [209–211]. Figure 8 shows the distribution of the microorganisms and enzymes used in processes where hybrid models were implemented (no matter if the goal was cell cultivation or metabolite production). Saccharomyces cerevisiae is the most studied microorganism with the largest number of applications coming from ethanol production or cell cultivation [67, 78, 131, 135, 170, 173, 202, 212–216]. Then, E. coli which has been mainly used for antibody and protein production [99, 151, 194, 217–220], has also been used for producing antivenom [221]. CHO has been mainly used in therapeutic production processes [51, 100, 122, 146, 199–201], with the three accounting for more than half of all applications. Pichia pastoris has been studied mainly for protein production [188, 195, 222], whereas Zymomonas mobilis has been used to describe sorbitol production [184] and ethanol production [174, 175]. The label “Bacteria” refers to unspecified bacteria, usually associated with mixed cultures in WWT [223, 224], but also Enterobacter A47 to produce exopolysaccharides [225], or the production of bacterial cellobiose by Acetobacter xylinum [226]. The category “Other” encompasses 32 different microorganisms and includes MA-104 (epithelial cells from the kidney of an African green monkey) for vaccine development [227], Kluyveromyces lactis for producing galactooligosaccharides [123], Xanthophyllomyces dendrorhous for producing astaxanthin [149], mixed microbial cultures for producing polyhydroxyalkanoates [228], Yarrowia lipolytica for citrate production [145], Cunninghamella echinulata for linolenic acid production [183], Pseudomonas putida used in the production of polyhydroxyalkanoates [229], Aspergillus niger in a sodium gluconate fermentation [132], Ralstonia eutropha in the production of poly-β-hydroxybutyrate [230], Candida rugosa in the production of lipase [198] among others.

### 4.3. Type of Data and Mode of Operation

Most of the hybrid models’ applications use experimental data for their development (80% of the total). The remaining 20% of the contributions use simulated data, usually derived from other mechanistic models such as the production of gluconic acid by Pseudomonas ovalis [231], describing the interactions between

It is important to note that hybrid models trained on simulated data can present a high level of bias because of the propagation error of the models used for producing the data. Pilot scale WWT data have been used to build soft sensors for modeling the phosphorous removal in a biofilm reactor [116], prediction of effluent quality in an activated sludge reactor, and control of critical parameters in an alternating aerobic-anoxic WWT plant [166]. At industrial scales, there are several applications for cell cultivation of S. cerevisiae [78, 239] and a CHO cultivation process [240]. ### 4.4. Computational Aspects

Only around 40.3% of the documents report on the software used for implementing the hybrid models. Figure 10 at the left shows the distribution of software, whereas on the right a cross-reference of the software and the nonparametric structures is shown as described in Figure 4. ANNs are the preferred nonparametric structure used in every software, followed by Regression techniques. Genetic algorithms were found only in MATLAB applications whereas Python presents several ML techniques, primarily developed in TensorFlow, PyTorch and Sci-kit learn packages. Most of the hybrid models have been implemented in MATLAB [17, 59, 99, 164, 244–246], with Python rising in recent years [122, 147, 209, 220]. Some applications have been developed in software like C# [241], Julia [131], Statistica [163, 181], or FORTRAN [74, 247]. Figure 11 shows the performance indicators for evaluating hybrid model’s fit. The most used performance indicator is the family of the MSE, which encompasses 45% of the occurrences (244 performance indicators used to evaluate models). Authors have used MSE in various forms, such as ROOT MSE (RMSE), normalized MSE (NMSE), RMSE of predicted values (RMSEP), weighted MSE (WMSE), and base MSE among others. The second most used indicator is r2 (Coefficient of determination), appearing in 25% of the applications, even though it may not be suitable for many non-linear problems. The Information Criteria (IC) such as Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) or Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) are very useful for determining the structure of the nonparametric sub model [11, 57]. Errors such as MAPE, MAE, mean relative error (MRE), mean average error (MAER), residual standard error (RSE), and mean relative percentage error (MRPE) make up almost 11% of the instances. The “Other” category is dominated by sum of squared errors (SSE) and residual standard deviation (RSD).

### 4.5. Recent Trends

Recent applications of hybrid modeling include the work of [248], where the authors use Bayesian inference applied to a Neural Network designed to predict both the reaction rates and stoichiometry from simulated data. They compare their results to a

AIC, Akaike Information Criterion; BIC, Bayesian Information Criterion; IC, Information Criteria; MAE, mean absolute error; MAER, mean average error; MAPE, mean absolute percentage error; MRE, mean relative error; MRPE, Mean relative percentage error; MSE, mean squared error; NMSE, normalized MSE; RMSE, root MSE; RMSEP, of predicted values; RSD, residual standard deviation; RSE, residual standard error; SSE, sum of squared errors; WMSE, weighted MSE.

pure data-driven technique, obtaining narrower confidence intervals and better prediction capabilities. The production of threonine applying Deep Learning techniques for the nonparametric model, obtains low errors when compared to the synthetic ANN training dataset [125]. Deep Learning was also applied to model a 50 L Pichia pastoris cultivation, increasing prediction accuracy by 18.4% and reducing CPU time by 43.4% when compared to a shallow ANN [238]. Hybrid models have proven to perform better

for antibody production than traditional parametric models [24, 102, 249]. A hybrid model was developed using data from 300 mL flasks and applied to describe the process in a 15 L bioreactor, with the error being in the same range as the analytical error and that of a traditional regression model [100]. A 100 kilogallons fermenter has been recently studied [126]. The authors carry out a sensitivity analysis of the traditional kinetic model to better understand which factors affect the output the most. The identified kinetic parameters are selected as candidates to be modeled using a Deep Neural Network. Of the candidates, a clustering analysis is done to identify those that vary with time, and the ones that have time dependence were selected as the parameters to be modeled by the nonparametric structure. The resultant hybrid model outperforms the traditional kinetic model, reducing the RMSE by a factor of 10. Some authors have used hybrid models to infer the structure of the mechanistic model [105]. A hybrid model using RL to regress the kinetic parameters for two proposed parametric structures was developed. The used framework correctly identified that a Monod-like kinetic structure was wrong because the parameter values were 0. In the same study, the authors trained a hybrid model on synthetic data (generated using the identified models) which predicted time-variant kinetic parameters, achieving a MAPE lower than 5% for an experimental batch run. Finally, they investigated the effect of noise in the hybrid model’s prediction. The MAPE deteriorated to 17% when 30% noise was added, indicating that the proposed framework can deal appropriately with noisy data. β-carotene production using Saccharomyces cerevisiae has been studied [131]. The authors used a Universal Differential Equation (UDE) to develop their hybrid model. In the UDE approach, a neural ordinary differential (an ordinary differential equation that is described by a neural network) equation that approximates the derivatives of the previously unknown dynamics of the batch fermentation process is integrated with the ordinary differential equations (ODEs) of its kinetic model to give a hybrid model with superior accuracy. The UDE model is compared with a traditional kinetic model, resulting in better predictions and lower MSE. Their work shows that neural ODEs can be integrated into hybrid models to describe kinetic parameters and their changes over time. The level of “grayness” in hybrid models was investigated by [183] in a Cunninghamella echinulata fermentation. Experiments were carried out at a 1 L fermentation and the models were tested in a 5 L bioreactor. Three hybrid models were developed, using GPs as a nonparametric structure, with an increasing degree of mechanistic knowledge in the kinetic expression. The model with the most mechanistic knowledge performed worse, indicating a high risk of inducing bias that hinders the model’s performance. The hybrid models showed similar performance in the 1 and the 5 L training datasets. The model with intermediate mechanistic knowledge performed better, with lower uncertainty and error. Introducing limited mechanistic knowledge resulted in overfitting issues. Their results show that incorporating kinetic knowledge that is not well understood can harm a hybrid model’s performance. A similar study was conducted in a CHO bioreactor [122]. Authors investigated several parametric and nonparametric techniques. However, they also investigated the “grayness” of hybrid models. Different hybrid models replacing one flux and up to five kinetic parameters predicted by the nonparametric technique were tested against an established parametric model. The hybrid models reproduced the design space, although on some edges the predictions were flatter than the ones given by the parametric model. Digital shadows, which are in silico representations of physical systems that capture and aggregate data from their real-world counterparts and have been built as a decision-making tool, present themselves as an emerging use case for hybrid models [250]. Recently, authors developed a digital shadow by coupling a mechanistic model with a purely data-driven soft sensor for estimating glucose and glycerol concentrations [119]. They studied a pilot (volumes of 550 and 2500 L) Aspergillus niger fermentation. The model was trained in 55 batch experiments with 4 additional calibration runs. To study scalability, 8 tests at the lab scale were performed. For the development of the data-driven soft sensor, a variety of models were tested, including ANNs, SVM, RF, Partial Least Squares, XGB, and LGBM. Their implementation achieved a normalized residual MSE of 2% with an r2 of 0.98. The model predicted biomass, glucose, and glycerol concentrations accurately for the three scales, indicating that hybrid models could be developed in smaller scales and later implemented in bigger scales, and still retain high prediction accuracy. Hybrid models have been recently used to accelerate the design and optimization of monoclonal antibody production [191]. The methodology used in silico experimental runs with a model derived by other authors [251]. The in silico experiments were used to train a hybrid model that follows a “feature learning” design pattern that uses an ANN as a nonparametric component. After the hybrid model training, a genetic algorithm was used to optimize the feeding schedule that maximizes the antibody titer at harvest, and after identifying the optimal conditions, another in silico experiment was run to assess the reliability of the predicted values. This strategy was compared to a traditional response surface methodology optimization strategy. The hybrid model correctly identified the optimal feeding strategy within 1% of the real strategy and showed a 34.9% increase in antibody titer when compared to training data and a 2.8% higher concentration than the optimal results from traditional response surface methodology. However, the predicted titer of the hybrid model was 18.6% lower than the real one, because the authors were extrapolating the hybrid model outside of its training region. Adding one more in silico experiment that covered the extrapolation region reduced the prediction error to 8.7%. LSTMs have been recently applied to model a downstream separation in an industrial biorefinery manufacturing 1,4-bio-butanediol [162]. The authors utilized a PLS model for estimating trans-membrane pressure, which was then coupled with a mechanistic knowledge model that follows Darcy’s equation, in a “feature learning” design pattern. The mechanistic knowledge model estimated the membrane resistances, and the hybrid model was deployed to predict short-term and long-term fouling of membranes, achieving r2 higher than 0.9. The authors claim that the model can identify irreversible and reversible

fouling, allowing for better analysis of performance and more in-depth diagnostics. Hybrid models have been used in genome-scale metabolic modeling to optimize ethanol production using S. cerevisiae [142]. Authors propose a hybrid model-driven platform that integrates flux balance analysis and several ML techniques, such as SVM, MLPs, RFs, and several linear regression techniques. The study highlights the importance of combining metabolic modeling and ML to unravel the complex relationships between genotype, phenotype, and the environment. The hybrid model identified key genetic modifications, including the overexpression of six target genes and the knockout of seven target genes, which significantly improved ethanol yield. Experiments showed that knocking out succinate dehydrogenase genes increased ethanol production by 6%–10% compared to the wild-type strain. Further dual-gene deletion experiments targeting glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and succinate dehydrogenase resulted in even higher ethanol yields, with improvements of up to 27.9%. Recently, dynamic modeling encompassing first principles and recurrent neural networks (RNN-LSTM) has been developed to enhance the sporulation process of Bacillus licheniformis BF-002 [204]. This innovative approach aimed to improve spore production by optimizing cultivation conditions, including carbon/nitrogen source feeding rates, pH, temperature, and agitation speed. The researchers cultivated the strain in a 5 L fermenter. The hybrid model was implemented in a “feature learning” design pattern: a traditional dynamic model that described the temporal variations of vegetative cell quantity and nutrient concentrations during growth and sporulation, and an RNN-LSTM model that predicted kinetic parameters dynamically influenced by environmental conditions. The hybrid model achieved a reduction of MRE of up to 82% in the number of vegetative cell quantities and 22% in the spore quantities when compared to a parametric model. The hybrid model was used with genetic algorithms to find the optimal feeding conditions that maximize spore production. This approach resulted in a 35.21% increase in sporulation, highlighting its effectiveness in optimizing cultivation dynamics. Transfer learning approaches have been recently implemented to take advantage of existing knowledge of one CHO process to another [146]. Authors used MLPs, RFs, XGBoost to predict kinetic parameters in a “feature learning” design pattern. There were two sets of experiments that produced different antibodies. One set was used for training and calibrating the hybrid models (dataset A) and the other was used for testing the transfer learning capabilities (dataset B). To correctly identify the adequate inputs to the nonparametric techniques, a series of correlation analyses and multi-collinearity were performed, to minimize the number of inputs that need to be measured. The three hybrid models perform similarly in the test experiments in dataset A, with an NRMSE of 0.07. In dataset B, predictions had slightly higher NRMSE (less than 0.02), with RFs performing the best. Authors also investigated performance when training the hybrid models in dataset B; however, they observed that the cumulative amount of glucose predictions did not improve, contrary to viable cell density and titer. Neural ODEs are used as expansion for non-accounted dynamics in the structure of parametric models [214]. The authors carried out experimental fed-batch cultivations using an engineered β-carotene producing S. cerevisiae strain. Over 50 parametric model structures were tested, identifying the best one. After identifying the best parametric structure, the Neural ODEs were implemented as an additive term to the ODEs describing biomass growth and ethanol production. The hybrid model exhibited 3.6-fold and 1.7-fold better performance in the training and testing datasets, when compared to the best parametric model structure. Despite longer training and calibration times than the parametric model, the hybrid model executed faster. There is a growing interest in applying hybrid modeling for commercial and industrial uses, with AspenTech filing for a patent [252, 253], the foundation of companies specialized in the area like DataHow AG and Novasign, and a recent interest on behalf of the pharmaceutical industry [59, 99, 101, 102].

### 4.6. Synthesis of Key Findings

Hybrid models in bioprocesses predominantly employ ANNs as the data-driven component, accounting for 58% of publications. ANNs have been widely applied across various bioprocesses, from cell cultivation to pharmaceutical production. Other ML techniques, such as SVMs, have also been utilized, particularly in cell cultivation and WTT. In lesser proportion, parametric techniques such as polynomials and sigmoidal expressions have been applied successfully to metabolic fluxes analysis [136], and lutein production [139]. From an application perspective, various categories of data-driven techniques have been successfully employed in bioprocessing. However, there is no consensus on the most suitable method for each process type, despite a clear preference for ANNs. Over 63% of work targets metabolite production—chiefly fermentation and protein synthesis—while ̃40% address pharmaceutical operations (penicillin, therapeutic proteins, antibodies, CHO cells) [101, 102]. As such, the enhanced prediction capabilities of hybrid models combined with specific approaches to experimental design [59, 98, 99] have led to innovation in the field. WTT comprises ̃10% of cases but leads in industrial uptake, underscoring hybrid models’ aptitude for revealing hidden dynamics under sparse monitoring. In terms of hybrid model architecture, feature learning hybrids dominate despite offering no statistically significant performance advantage over delta or serial patterns. Their popularity likely stems from built-in interpretability, conservation law enforcement, and modular training, which suit the multi-step, partially observed nature of bioprocesses [20]. Ethanol fermentations of S. cerevisiae remain the most intensely studied system—driven by abundant data—while recent work has diversified to include E. coli, P. pastoris, CHO cells (collectively 30%), and a broad “other” category (32%). Studies equally showcase hybrid models across batch (44.6%), fed batch (33.7%) and continuous (20.7%) modes of operation and at lab (53%), pilot (25%) and industrial (21.7%) scales, underscoring their adaptability [119].

Software choice and model evaluation are areas of persistent inconsistency. MATLAB remains the predominant simulation environment, although Python is gaining traction. Model performance assessment still is variant: about a quarter of studies still rely on r2 —despite its failure to penalize over parameterization and insensitivity to nonlinear dynamics [94, 254]. On the other hand, 45% of contributions use MSE derivatives to calculate their performance indexes, despite it being highly sensitive to outliers [255]. This last selection might be since it is a default performance index in ML toolboxes. To foster more robust and interpretable assessments, we foresee that these performance indexes could be complemented with information-theoretic and distribution-based measures (e.g., entropy coefficients, Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics, Log-Cosh and quantile losses) and adopting principled model-comparison criteria such as Watanabe Akaike Information Criterion (WAIC) or Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation Information Criterion (LOO-CVI) [256–259]. Despite three decades of development, hybrid bioprocess modeling still lacks standardized protocols for selecting design patterns, balancing mechanistic and data-driven components, quantifying uncertainty and defining data preprocessing workflows. The field’s reliance on trial and error and experience—evidenced by 374 individual model implementations versus 155 distinct case studies—underscores this gap. Some efforts have been made recently to highlight practical and technical details of implementing hybrid models, such as reviews that present brief guides for developing them [25, 260], but more work is needed. Due to having both a parametric/mechanistic component and a data-driven/nonparametric component, assessing how much uncertainty comes from each remains an unexplored avenue. The field could benefit from recent developments in the ML field, where authors suggest a Monte Carlo approach to generate testing datasets and better capture uncertainty [261]. The absence of standardized guidelines in hybrid bioprocess modeling arises precisely from its defining strength: structural flexibility. Hybrid frameworks can accommodate a wide range of design choices—yet still outperform purely mechanistic models—while demanding far less data than fully nonparametric approaches and preserving a degree of interpretability that renders them practical for industrial deployment. However, this very hybrid character also complicates evaluation: conventional metrics and workflows developed for parametric or nonparametric models often fail to capture the unique tradeoffs in uncertainty quantification and mechanistic parameter estimation inherent to hybrid systems. Numerical workflows in hybrid bioprocess modeling are similarly under specified. Critical steps—data pretreatment methods (both numerical and knowledge based), augmentation strategies, and the rationale for selecting inputs to the data driven module—are frequently omitted, leaving reproducibility and comparability in doubt. Moreover, cross-validation protocols and data partitioning schemes are rarely described, despite their importance for robust training and unbiased assessment of models that rely heavily on high-quality data to capture complex, industrially relevant dynamics. To address these gaps, the community should adopt rigorous information-theoretic tools to quantify intervariable relationships and guide model structure, and standardize transparent cross-validation procedures to ensure reliable, reproducible hybrid model development [262]. Cross validation offers clear advantages—correcting selection bias, quantifying estimation uncertainty (particularly for nonparametric components) and guiding model complexity to prevent overfitting [263]. Yet, despite its value, consensus on hyperparameter tuning remains elusive. While many practitioners adhere to the conventional three-way split (training, validation, test) coupled with grid, random or Bayesian searches, limited data often forces a two-set approach (training and validation only). Without systematic cross validation, hybrid models inherit latent selection bias, further obscuring true predictive uncertainty. Although a handful of specialized diagnostic tools exist for assessing hybrid performance, the community still lacks standardized protocols for data partitioning and hyperparameter optimization—an important frontier for improving both transparency and reliability in hybrid bioprocess modeling. The challenges outlined above often originate in insufficient data quantity and quality, underscoring the necessity of integrating hybrid-model data requirements into the experimental design phase. In this context, Intensified Design of Experiments (iDoE) offers a compelling solution: by strategically varying inputs and conditions, iDoE minimizes the total number of trials while maximizing the informational content of each run, thereby furnishing richer datasets that better support the calibration and validation of hybrid bioprocess models [59, 98, 99, 117]. Of course, this strategy is also limited by monitoring capabilities, since online data acquisition of primary variables at high frequency still is a challenge. Developments in process analytical technologies (PAT) definitely will catalyze the advanced modeling strategies as hybrid models.

### 4.7. Hybrid Modeling Challenges

Certain challenges for implementing hybrid models have been mentioned in the literature [26, 55, 264]:

1. The mechanistic part of the hybrid model constrains the

space of solutions obtainable, which helps avoid pitfalls such as negative concentrations. These constraints impose an inductive bias into the responses, which might negatively affect the hybrid model’s performance if the mechanistic part is not suitable for describing the process.

2. There are standard techniques for identifying parameters

in statistical or purely parametric models. For hybrid models, only a handful of parameter identification methods have been reported [57, 95, 104, 265]. The major hurdle is the time needed for parameter identification, due to the extensive calculations that should be performed.

3. In addressing the initial challenge, the integration of hybrid

models requires a thorough examination of the foundational assumptions inherent in the mechanistic knowledge to be integrated. This task can be approached via two distinct methodologies:

a. The incremental approach, where the most basic

assumptions are made, and more complex interactions are added until the model performance decreases.

b. The removal approach, where the most complex funda-

mental structure is evaluated first, and then features are removed iteratively to determine what part is hindering the model’s performance. Both approaches are time consuming, so model development will require some experience or an analysis of a risk of mechanistic knowledge being incorrect.

4. Validating and verifying a hybrid model is another chal-

lenge, because there needs to be a balance of complexity, accuracy, interpretability and scalability which is hard to optimize. Moreover, in hybrid models, nonparametric and parametric components can introduce distinct sources of uncertainty and error that must be carefully managed [26].

5. The level of “grayness” in hybrid models—the bal-

ance between mechanistic knowledge and data-driven components—can significantly impact performance. As illustrated by Rogers et al. [183], incorporating too much or too little mechanistic knowledge can lead to bias or overfitting, respectively, thus hindering model performance. This underscores the need for meticulous calibration and validation of hybrid models to ensure optimal balance and performance. Regardless of advancements in key areas, still there is not a unified framework for determining the valid region for extrapolation of hybrid models. Besides the challenges addressed before, we propose the following ones that emerge from the literature review:

1. There are no consumer-ready applications built on

open-source software for building hybrid models easily, which hinders its adoption by industry, due to the need for specialized personnel to build, operate and maintain the models. Although some custom toolboxes for MATLAB like HYBMOD [125, 220, 222, 233] exist, source code is poorly documented, and a licensing agreement should be signed.

2. As with many pure data-driven techniques, there is not

a consolidated framework that allows to select the proper nonparametric technique a priori, meaning that a costly process of trial and error is necessary to build hybrid models.

3. Like the previous challenge, there is a lack of a general and

unified framework for deciding which type of hybrid model structure/design pattern is best suited for an application, which also results in a resource-intensive search.

4. As with many nonparametric techniques, how data should

be split between training, testing and validations has no consensus. Authors commonly only use training and validation splits due to constraints on the availability of high-quality data, while few report using datasets for the three purposes.

5. There is no consensus on the training hierarchy of the para-

metric and nonparametric components of hybrid models. When using the “delta model” design pattern, the training of each subcomponent is done separately. However, when using the other design patterns, there are no clear guidelines on how to address the identification of the parametric components and the nonparametric components of hybrid models. Some authors choose the best pure parametric model structure available, start hybridizing and then calibrating the nonparametric structure over it [214]. Other authors do the calibration of both components at the same time [266, 267]. Whether one approach yields better results than the other needs to be further investigated.

### 4.8. Hybrid Modeling Perspectives

Looking forward, several promising avenues for future research and development in hybrid semi-parametric modeling are clear. One key area is the continued refinement of model integration techniques. Advancements and applications of deep learning [125, 220, 222] and the development of sophisticated neural network architectures offer opportunities to enhance the nonparametric components of hybrid models. The application of Bayesian inference, could improve the accuracy and confidence of predictions by incorporating uncertainty quantification into the modeling process [248]. Additionally, expanding the application of hybrid models to new bioprocesses and products will be crucial. As the bioprocessing industry continues to innovate and develop new products, hybrid models will need to adapt and evolve to meet these emerging challenges. The growing interest from commercial and industrial sectors, including companies like AspenTech and DataHow AG, as well as the pharmaceutical industry, further underscores the relevance and applicability of hybrid models in real-world settings. The development of standardized frameworks and best practices for hybrid model implementation could facilitate broader adoption and integration into industrial processes. Authors should remain open-minded and explore solutions and implementations beyond hybrid modeling in bioprocesses or applied mathematics or computer science; for instance, disciplines like agriculture and meteorology have yielded promising hybrid modeling strategies [268–270]. Although implementations are dependent on data quality and specific to each field, general insights and strategies can be adapted. Hybrid semi-parametric models represent a powerful tool for advancing bioprocess modeling and optimization. Integrating mechanistic and data-driven approaches offers a pathway to more accurate, reliable, and scalable models that can meet the complex demands of modern bioprocessing. Continued research and innovation in this field will undoubtedly unlock new opportunities and enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of bioprocesses across various industries.

## 5. Concluding Remarks

This work presents a comprehensive framework for hybrid modeling in bioprocesses, drawing insights from 270 references. It covers hybrid models’ characteristics, architecture, and nonparametric structures. Hybrid models are primarily

applied to metabolite production, especially ethanol and penicillin fermentations—followed by cell cultivation and WTT. In protein production, antibody manufacturing is significant. ANNs are the dominant nonparametric method, though other ML techniques such as random processes and genetic algorithms are also used. Most models are trained on experimental data from laboratory-scale studies, with some full-scale industrial applications. Batch and fed-batch systems are the most common operation modes, while continuous processes are less explored. Frequently used microorganisms include Saccharomyces cerevisiae, E. coli, and CHO cells. MATLAB is the preferred software, though Python is gaining popularity due to its robust ML toolboxes. Finally, while MSE and related metrics are common, no consensus exists on how to best evaluate hybrid model performance. PSE provides the critical link between these hybrid-model capabilities and global sustainability imperatives. By embedding life-cycle assessment, techno-economic analysis and multi-objective optimization within hybrid modeling workflows, PSE enables quantitative trade-off studies that reconcile yield, energy consumption, emissions and cost from early design through scale-up. Digital-twin simulations and real-time soft sensors further ensure adaptive control and resilience under variable feedstocks. Such integrated PSE-driven approaches directly support UN SDG 7 (clean energy), SDG 9 (industry and innovation), SDG 12 (responsible production) and SDG 13 (climate action) by valorizing biomass waste, minimizing environmental impact and fostering low-carbon biomanufacturing. Standardizing PSE-embedded sustainability metrics within hybrid models will be pivotal for accelerating tangible SDG progress and closing the financing and implementation gaps that currently jeopardize the 2030 agenda.
